title: How airlines really make money (it isn't the seats)

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Rohan just paid {seat_amount} for this flight. The airline's profit on his seat? About {seat_per_period}. The real money went somewhere else: through his card, and into a bank.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Hold on. That little? Then why does every airline keep begging me to sign up for its credit card?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Six ways an airline makes money. The seat. The fare ladder. The fees. The cargo under your feet. The miles. And the last one, the bank hiding inside the airline.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: And by the end, you'll know who really pays for every free flight. Hint: it might be you.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Way one. The seat.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Start with the ticket. Rohan paid {seat_amount} for one seat on one flight.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Out of that fare comes the fuel, the crew's pay, the airport fees and the plane itself.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Fuel alone can eat around a quarter of an airline's costs, and no airline controls the price of oil.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: After all of it, an airline keeps about {seat_fee_pct} of the fare as profit. On Rohan's ticket, that's {seat_per_period}.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: That's about the price of a sandwich at the gate.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Airlines run on thin margins. One bad year of fuel prices, a strike or a storm season, and the profit is simply gone.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: Warren Buffett once joked that a smart investor at Kitty Hawk should have shot the first plane down.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: So why run an airline at all? Because the seat isn't really the product. It's the doorway.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And not every seat sells for {seat_amount}. The woman beside Rohan paid far less, for the very same seat.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Way two. The fare ladder.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Way two starts at the departures board. One flight, and a whole ladder of prices.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Priya booked this flight months ahead. She paid {fare_amount}.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Rohan booked last week, for the seat right beside hers. His fare: {fare_final}.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: That's {fare_gains} more for the identical trip. Rohan's fare is {fare_ratio} hers.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: I paid more than double for the exact same seat? Next to her?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Airlines sell every flight in buckets. The cheapest bucket sells out first, then the next, and the price of every bucket keeps climbing.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Software watches every booking. When seats sell fast, the price jumps. When they sell slowly, a sale appears.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: So the price I pay depends on when I happen to look?

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: And on how badly you need to go. The system can't read your mind, but it can read the calendar.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: Before the software, a ticket had one price on a paper coupon. Now one flight can carry dozens of prices at once.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Fly on a quiet Tuesday instead of a busy Friday, and the very same seat can cost less.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Who buys the top bucket? People who must fly: business trips, family emergencies, plans made the night before.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: School holidays, a festival, a big game in town: the moment demand jumps, every bucket climbs with it.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: The cheap seats fill the plane. The expensive ones pay for it.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: That's why I book early. The cheap bucket is built for people who plan.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: But the fare is only the price you see up front. The next way waits for Rohan at the check-in desk.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Way three. The fees.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: At the desk, Rohan's suitcase costs extra. So does a seat with legroom, and the snack on board.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: On the cheapest tickets, even sitting next to your own family can cost extra.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: I have to pay to sit next to my own mother?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Say his extras add {extras_per_period} to the trip. That's {fees_diff} more than the airline's profit on his whole seat.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Fees aren't pure profit. But a bag in a hold that's flying anyway costs the airline far less than it charges.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: The ticket is the bait, my friend. The extras are the meal.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: When did bags stop flying for free? I remember when they just did.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: In America, around the time fuel prices spiked. The fuel came down. The bag fees stayed.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Airlines call it unbundling. The low fare gets you through the door. Everything else is sold piece by piece.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Airlines in America collect billions of dollars a year from bag fees alone.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: The very cheapest tickets often come with the fewest rights: no seat choice, no changes, sometimes not even a big cabin bag.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And if Rohan's plans change, the cheapest fare may not let him change a thing. He buys a whole new ticket.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: And the scramble for overhead space? Plenty of people are just dodging the checked-bag fee.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: That's why the fare on the first screen is the least useful number. The whole trip is the real one.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Add it all up, and Rohan's bargain fare is not much of a bargain any more.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Bag after bag, flight after flight, those little fees pile into a mountain.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: So the cheap fare was never the real price. Got it.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Three ways so far: the seat, the fare and the fees. All small. The next one is riding right under Rohan's feet.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Way four. The cargo.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Three ways are on the board. The fourth is hiding under the floor of the plane.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Below the cabin floor is the hold. Next to the suitcases ride crates, parcels and sacks of mail.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: A big passenger jet can carry tons of freight below the cabin, on almost every trip it flies.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Companies pay to ship their goods on a plane that was flying that route anyway.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Take one full flight: {flight_parts} seats at {flight_per_part} is {flight_total} of fares. Say cargo adds another {cargo_fee_pct} on top. That's {cargo_per_period}.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: In the pandemic, some airlines flew planes with no passengers at all. Only cargo.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: When nobody could travel, the parcels kept some of those planes in the air.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Post offices pay airlines to carry mail, too. A letter sent abroad often rides in the hold of a passenger flight.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Online shopping made it bigger. A phone ordered tonight on the other side of the world can fly under passengers within days.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: So my suitcase shares a ride with someone's online shopping.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: A parcel's day: the warehouse, the airport, the hold under Rohan's seat, and a doorstep on the other side of the world within days.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: Cargo is quiet money. Nobody posts about a parcel's flight.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Every empty corner of the hold is space the airline can sell, on a trip it was making anyway.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Four ways down, and none of them is the big one. The big one is sitting in Rohan's wallet.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Way five. The miles.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Every flight earns Rohan miles. Here's the strange part: the airline can create as many miles as it likes.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: In effect, an airline prints its own money. And then it sells that money to banks.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: A bank buys miles by the billion, to hand out on the airline's credit card.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And not only to banks. Airlines sell miles to hotels, car rental firms and shops: anyone who wants to reward a customer.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Why would a bank pay for miles? Because miles make people swipe, and every swipe pays the bank.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Each time Rohan pays with the card, the shop pays a swipe fee: an assumed {swipe_fee_pct} of the bill.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: He spends {swipe_amount} a month on the card. That's {swipe_per_period} of swipe fees every month, and {swipe_per_year_total} a year, from just one card.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Part of that fee comes back to Rohan as miles. The rest stays with the bank, which bought those miles from the airline.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: And that's one shopper. Now multiply him by millions of cardholders.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: Banks buy the miles, and the miles bring them customers. Customers who swipe and swipe.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: One of America's biggest airlines reports getting billions of dollars a year from its card partner. Not from flights. From a bank.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Banks often pay the airline extra for every new cardholder who signs up. That's why the crew sometimes walk the aisle with card offers.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: That's why they keep begging me to sign up. It was never about the flight.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: So when I swipe for groceries, an airline gets paid?

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Through the bank, yes. Your weekly shop is part of the airline business now.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And many miles are never spent at all. They expire, or sit forgotten in old accounts. The industry has a word for it: breakage.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: A mile sold and never spent is money the airline never has to give back in seats.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: A mile costs the airline very little to create. It only costs a seat when someone spends it, often a seat that would have flown empty.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: The airline can also change what a mile buys. Ask for more miles for the same seat, and everyone's miles quietly shrink.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: So my miles are a currency the airline can shrink whenever it wants?

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Like any currency. Except this one has one central bank, and it's the airline.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Year one, Rohan's swipes send {swipe_per_year_total} through the system. Year five, the same again. After {swipe_years} years, {swipe_total}, from one ordinary shopper.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: So that's five ways: seats, fares, fees, cargo and miles. But someone has to pay for all those free flights. The last way shows who.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Way six. The bank inside the airline.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Five ways so far, all lined up. Before the sixth, Rohan has a question.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Fine. Then who's paying for all these free flights?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Here's the twist. Those free flights aren't free. The shop pays the swipe fee, then builds it into its prices, for everyone. Even the people paying cash.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: Shops don't swallow that fee. They price it in. Groceries, coffee, fuel: a little higher for everyone.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Economists at the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston found that people paying cash end up helping fund card rewards.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And the fancier the card, the bigger the swipe fee the shop usually pays on it.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And anyone who carries a balance pays interest, often far more than the rewards they earn.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: So the people paying for my free flight might be the ones who can least afford it.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: That doesn't make the card a scam. It means the rewards are paid for. Just not always by the person earning them.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: The winners: people who pay in full and actually use the perks. The losers: people who pay interest, and people who pay cash.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Now follow all of those payments. The swipe fees, the sign-ups, the annual fees. They flow into one place: the loyalty programme.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: That loyalty programme is where Rohan's miles live. Its members, its card deals and its partners are a business of their own.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: The bank pays for the miles. The airline keeps the cash. And the members keep chasing their next free flight.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: In the pandemic, with planes parked, big American airlines borrowed billions of dollars, and put up their loyalty programmes as security.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And the lenders valued those programmes at more than the whole airline was worth on the stock market.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Think about that. The whole company, planes and all, was valued at less than its points.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: So it's a bank. With some planes attached.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: The plane is the shop window. The loyalty programme is the bank behind it.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: In a bad year, the planes lose money. People still swipe their cards.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And Rohan pays to belong to that bank. His premium card charges an annual fee of {annual_amount}.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Over {annual_years} years, that's {annual_total} in fees alone, before he books a single seat.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Lounge visits, a free bag, a companion ticket. Each perk is only worth something if Rohan actually uses it.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: But I get lounge access and a free checked bag!

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: If you use them, they can be worth it. Lots of people pay for perks they never touch.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: So once a year, I do the sum: what did the card give me, and what did it cost me?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And if the perks don't beat the fee, about the same money, {invest_amount} a month, invested at an assumed {invest_rate}, could grow to {invest_final} in {invest_years} years.

params.title: The fee, or the fee invested

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: So Rohan makes one rule. The card is cash: he pays it off in full, every single month. That way the miles are his, and the interest is nobody's.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: Six ways to make money, and only one of them actually flies you anywhere.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Simplified maths with assumed margins, fees and returns. Would you still take the airline card? Comment below.

params.cta: Would you still take the airline card?
